body.text: Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
When the curtains close on the parliamentary year, the leaders of every party can walk away from Canberra feeling like they had a little win.
The government cleared almost everything it wanted off the legislative decks and, in the end, didn't even have to give up that much ground to do so.

Labor paired with the Greens for three out of four of the bills. On the Digital Duty of Care Bill, which puts the onus on big tech to prevent foreseeable harms, it agreed to substantially beef up the fines for social media platforms that breach that duty. Australians will also have the right to sue.

Communications Minister Anika Wells was jubilant on her victory lap. She laughed in the hallway, and hugged Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young on the floor of the Senate as applause broke out celebrating the bill's passage.
"Bring it on," was how she responded when asked if she was worried about a legal challenge.

But it was a social media post from Labor's Ellie Whiteaker that really set off some within Coalition ranks. The little-known senator linked the rise of tradwife content online and the Digital Duty of Care.
It culminated with a mid-week shouting match between Minister Clare O'Neil and Liberal frontbencher Michaelia Cash on breakfast television.
"Of course, tradwife content is not being banned, of course it's not," O'Neil said, as Cash repeated the well-trodden line that the government couldn't be trusted.
Before the legislation passed, the Coalition and One Nation had already declared they'd repeal the laws if elected.

It wasn't just the Digital Duty of Care that the government turned to the Greens for help with. It agreed to the minor party's demands over partially winding back a Howard-era private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 and over, foregoing half of the planned $3 billion in savings by carving out pensioners.
The Greens didn't get everything their own way. A push to make an exemption for charitable giving under Labor's 30 per cent minimum tax for discretionary trusts went unanswered.

But, in return, it got an opaque agreement that something would be done to make people with privately owned jets pay more on their registration fees, to make up for the low tax they pay on aviation fuel when compared to the tax regular motorists pay. The details are still TBC.

But Greens leader David Shoebridge will end the week feeling okay about where his party landed — they get to declare they pushed the government into action on tech giants and billionaires — and end the year being constructive rather than blocking.
'Labor on the rocks'

While the government had a number of political wins, it couldn't shake the economic woes. Treasurer Jim Chalmers's economic statement didn't paint a great picture of what's to come. The long of the short of it is things will get worse before they get better.

Cuts to the public service have been flagged as well as "reprofiling" in the infrastructure portfolio, as Chalmers continues to assure the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook will contain "modest saves".
The economic statement, paired with inflation jumping to 4.9 per cent in October, were easy pickings for the Coalition, who repeatedly asked when the prime minister would sack Chalmers.

Albanese won't do that, and instead repeatedly came to his treasurer's defence in Question Time. As Chalmers (who sits behind him) stared off into the middle distance, or looked at his phone, one could almost hear the attack lines forming in the Coalition's mind.

The only person having a worse time than Chalmers this week was probably Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who returned to the chamber still processing the breakdown in talks at the UN Climate Change summit, COP31.
For the Coalition, its wins weren't so much in the chamber but elsewhere.

Other than agreeing in the end to pass the gas reservation scheme, which will require Australia's largest exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their supply for the domestic market, the party wasn't in the negotiating frame.
Angus Taylor began the week buoyed by fresh opinion polling that again reported a lift in the Coalition's primary vote.
The party has been losing supporters to One Nation, so the latest numbers were a small mercy for an opposition leader who has often struggled to cut through.

Taylor rallied his troops by reminding them the government's rising unpopularity, paired with a grim economic outlook, has given the Coalition a fighting chance to be in it to win it come the next election.
"Labor is on the rocks. This government is on the rocks. Australians see this prime minister for who he is — a lying, arrogant, weak, incompetent prime minister," he said.
It's a far cry from the fat chance the opposition was given after Peter Dutton's drubbing last year.
A Blyth choice
But then One Nation decided to throw another spanner in the works.
Pauline Hanson fired up the sandwich press for her second annual defector dinner. The newest recruit? South Australian Liberal senator Leah Blyth.

Blyth offered a number of reasons why she wanted to make the switch. First, it was because the party had lost its way, pointing to the Coalition's decision to remain in the Paris Agreement despite walking away from net zero.

She cited not feeling safe in the party, before offering a lack of debate over laws that give the defence minister sweeping powers to designate areas for defence purposes as another reason for leaving. But it's a bill One Nation voted for.

The bit Blyth didn't say out loud was that it's a move in self-preservation, as Clare Armstrong wrote today. Blyth is up for re-election in 2028 and is unlikely to win a preselection battle for the top of the Senate ticket.
If the opinion polls stay where they are, and Blyth isn't at the top, she's unlikely to return to Canberra. Basically, it's the same reason Tammy Tyrrell made the shift to Labor earlier in the year.
The news of her departure caused a ripple, rather than a splash, across the Coalition. Scott Buchholz probably put it best when asked if it was a surprise.
"Yeah, of course it was," the Queensland MP said. "I have to go find out who she is now."
